correction.text: unchanged shape, valid 398-399 only; in 397 the page names only Jiankang

keyframe_review.note: 397-401, 119,670 km2 at 93.2-102.0 E, 38.4-41.0 N: Zhangye, Jiuquan and Dunhuang. The page names only Jiankang (397) and Zhangye (398, after Mengxun took 'several commanderies'); the Western Liang page shows Li Gao serving the Northern Liang as a magistrate and Administrator of Dunhuang, and Jiuquan and Liangning surrendering 'from Northern Liang' in 401, so the Hexi oases were Duan Ye's until then. The shape is kept for 398-399, with the oases leaving in 400 and 401 (northern-liang_400, _401). The infobox gives no area; ratio unavailable. [orchestrator 2 Nov 2026: from/to set to 398..399 from this entry's own 'valid 398-399 only'; without them the compiler drew the shape for all its Cliopatria years, overlapping the next keyframe (window p1100-p1199 report)]

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Li Gao was made Administrator of Dunhuang... Later that year, Tang Yao rebelled in Jinchang and acclaimed him; he 'rebelled against the Northern Liang and formed the Western Liang (400-421)' (Sixteen Kingdoms page). Dunhuang and Jinchang leave in 400.

What stays with Mengxun is the Zhangye strip.

It is right only for 421-425, when Mengxun held the whole corridor from Dunhuang to Zhangye, and then lacks Guzang: the Cliopatria shape stops at 102.0 E and never reaches Wuwei (102.6 E, 37.9 N), the capital from 412, while its Western Qin shape from 414 takes the Wuwei belt. Corrected for 421-425 by adding a disc at Wuwei; 402-410, 411-419 and 420 have their own keyframes. No infobox area.

correction.text: the Juqu holdout in the western Hexi oases, valid 439-440

keyframe_review.note: 439-440, 118,530 km2: Zhangye to Dunhuang without Guzang, which the Northern Wei took in 439 (so this shape is the Juqu holdout). The infobox has Jiuquan as capital in 440-441 and Dunhuang in 441-442, with the flight to Gaochang in 442, so the state lasts to 442; the shape is used for 439-440 and a Dunhuang disc for 441-442.

New keyframe for 441-442: the capital is Dunhuang (infobox 441-442) before the Juqu fled and occupied the oasis city of Gaochang in 442. Cliopatria's Northern Wei shape reaches 93 E in 441, so the Wei dossier ends the holdout a year earlier than the infobox.

region.text: the Jiankang commandery in the Zhangye region

ledger.note: 397: Duan Ye is installed at Jiankang as Northern Liang prince. In 397, Duan Ye is installed at Jiankang after the Juqu rebellion; real power was shared with Mengxun and Nancheng; the Sixteen Kingdoms page: 'Duan Ye, who established the Northern Liang (397-439)'.

region.text: Zhangye and the commanderies west of it as far as Dunhuang

ledger.note: 398: Mengxun takes Zhangye. 'In 398, Mengxun took several commanderies before capturing Zhangye', which becomes the capital. The page names no other commanderies; the region is the researcher's reading of Cliopatria's 397 shape.
398: the capital moves from Jiankang to Zhangye (infobox Zhangye 398-412).

400: Li Gao breaks away at Dunhuang. Li Gao was made Administrator of Dunhuang. Later that year, Tang Yao rebelled in Jinchang and acclaimed him, offering the title of Duke of Liang; the Sixteen Kingdoms page: he 'rebelled against the Northern Liang'.

region.text: Jiuquan commandery (the gazetteer lacks Jiuquan; Jiayuguan lies 25 km from it)

ledger.note: 401: Jiuquan and Liangning go to the Western Liang. 'In 401, both Jiuquan and Liangning... commanderies also surrendered to him from Northern Liang.' The same year Mengxun kills Nancheng and Duan Ye and takes power (Northern Liang page: 'In 401, Mengxun manoeuvred into killing Nancheng and Duan Ye').

region.text: Guzang (Wuwei), the Northern Liang's capital from 412

ledger.note: 411: Guzang surrenders to Mengxun. 'The inhabitants of Guzang later surrendered to him in 411' after the unsuccessful siege of 410. The Southern Liang page says Guzang fell to Northern Liang in 410.
412: Guzang becomes the capital: 'In 412, he made the city his new capital' and elevated himself to King of Hexi.

region.text: Jiuquan commandery (the gazetteer lacks Jiuquan; Jiayuguan lies 25 km from it)

ledger.note: 420: Jiuquan falls to the Northern Liang. Li Xin was lured into attacking Guzang and trapped; 'He died in battle, and Northern Liang forces soon captured Jiuquan.' The Northern Liang page: 'By 421, he captured their capital'.

421: Mengxun ends the Western Liang. 'The city eventually fell and Li Xun committed suicide in 421, putting an end to Western Liang.' The page does not name the city; the infobox has Dunhuang as the capital in 420-421, so it is read as Dunhuang. The Northern Liang page: 'By 421, he captured their capital' (Jiuquan) and ended the Western Liang. The whole corridor is now Northern Liang. Reviewer (ea-03-d): the Western Liang page has Li Xun succeed 'in Dunhuang' before 'the city eventually fell' in 421; confidence raised to 3.

region.text: Guzang (Wuwei) and eastern Hexi, as in the Northern Wei dossier

ledger.note: 439: Northern Wei takes Guzang and the Northern Liang is ended. 'In 439, alleging that Mujian was planning to rebel,' Wei besieged Guzang and 'Mujian surrendered himself to Wei, thus ending the Northern Liang.' The page gives no month.
440: the Juqu hold out in the west, with Jiuquan as capital (infobox Jiuquan 440-441). The page's text does not narrate the holdout.

441: the last Juqu seats in the western oases pass to Wei. Page silent on who took Jiuquan; the infobox moves the capital from Jiuquan to Dunhuang in 441, and the Northern Wei dossier gains the region in 441 from Cliopatria's Wei shape. Reviewer (ea-03-d): the Juqu Wuhui page dates it: 'In spring 440, Juqu Wuhui tried to recapture Jiuquan', 'soon capturing it', and 'by winter 441, Jiuquan fell to Northern Wei forces'; confidence raised to 2.
441: the capital moves to Dunhuang (infobox Dunhuang 441-442).

442: the Juqu abandon the Hexi. The Juqu fled and occupied Gaochang in 442; Dunhuang is the last seat (infobox 441-442), and the exile regime at Shanshan and Gaochang (442-460) is a separate state. Page silent on who took Dunhuang; the Wei dossier has the western Hexi in 441.

certainty.note: The Hexi corridor is a chain of oases between desert and mountains; the page names Jiankang, Zhangye, Guzang, Jiuquan and Dunhuang only and no frontier with the Tuyuhun, the Rouran or the Western Qin. No treaty line exists.

notes: Cliopatria row: Northern Liang 397..440, four shapes of about 119,000 km2, all the same Zhangye-Jiuquan-Dunhuang outline at 93.2-102.0 E. (1) The shape never includes Guzang (Wuwei), the capital from 412; its Western Qin shape takes the Wuwei belt from 414 to 438, the Later Liang's 400 shape and the Later Qin's 410-413 shape. All four shapes are therefore corrected: 397-399 as drawn, 400 minus Dunhuang, 401-410 the Zhangye strip, 411-419 plus Guzang, 420 plus Jiuquan, 421-438 the whole corridor, 439-440 the holdout, 441-442 Dunhuang. The Western Qin and Later Qin dossiers need to follow (Later Qin gives Hexi away in 412 at confidence 1, the Southern Liang page has Guzang given in 406). (2) End year: the page says 'ending the Northern Liang' in 439 but the infobox gives Jiuquan 440-441 and Dunhuang 441-442 as capitals and the flight to Gaochang in 442; the dossier ends in 442 and the Northern Wei dossier gains the holdout in 441 (conf 1); one of the two years should be settled. (3) Page disagreements: Guzang lost 410 (Southern Liang) or surrendered 411 (Northern Liang); Jiuquan captured in 420 (Western Liang) or 'by 421' (Northern Liang). (4) Infobox lists predecessors Later Liang, Southern Liang, Western Qin and successors Northern Wei, Gaochang: only the Later Liang gives land at the start; the exile regime at Shanshan and Gaochang (442-460) needs its own dossier (slug northern-liang-of-gaochang; the kingdom-of-gaochang dossier starts in 460). (5) Vassalage (suzerain's dossier owns it): the infobox lists Later Qin, Eastern Jin, Northern Wei and Liu Song; the page has Mengxun a Wei vassal after 431 and the Liu Song confirming his title in 423. The Northern Wei dossier has no vassal event for it. (6) The Tuyuhun and Rouran, listed as Cliopatria neighbours, are not mentioned on the page. (7) The gazetteer lacks Jiuquan, Jinchang (the ancient commandery; the modern city of that name is elsewhere) and Jiankang (the commandery, not Nanjing); Zhangye stands for Jiankang and Jiayuguan for Jiuquan. No infobox area, so the factor-of-two check could not be made. Page budget: five pages.
